analysis.one_liner: Requires states to draw congressional districts through independent commissions and bans mid-decade redistricting.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, drew zero cosponsors, and never received a vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would take the drawing of congressional district maps away from state legislators and give it to an independent commission in each state. Commissions would have to hold public meetings, post their data and maps online, and follow rules like keeping counties and neighborhoods together and ignoring party affiliation and where incumbents live. States would also be barred from redrawing their congressional map more than once after each census, unless a court orders it, and federal money would help pay for the commissions.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters in states where legislators currently draw their own district lines, including the nearly all of states that lack an independent commission. Fairer, more compact districts and a ban on mid-decade remapping would make elections more competitive and make members of Congress answer to voters rather than to the legislators who draw their districts. Voters get public meetings, online mapping tools, and the right to submit their own plans. The small number of states that already use commissions would see their systems recognized in federal law.

how_it_helps.text: Every state would have to draw its congressional map through an independent commission rather than the legislature, with members barred from having held office or party jobs in the prior four years and barred from running for Congress afterward [S3].

The commission could not consider voters' party affiliation, voting history, or where incumbents live when drawing districts, and must prioritize keeping counties, municipalities, and neighborhoods whole and districts compact and contiguous [S3].
States could redraw congressional maps only once after each census, ending mid-decade remapping, except when a court orders a redraw to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act [S2].

Commissions would have to meet in public, run a website with census data and interactive software so anyone can draft and submit a competing map, and hold hearings around the state before finalizing a plan [S3].

If a legislature rejects the commission's plan, the state's highest court could pick from commission-drawn plans, and if no state commission exists or no plan is chosen, a federal district court draws the map under the same rules [S3].
The federal government would pay states $150,000 per House seat to run their commissions, conditioned on actually establishing one [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers fund the commissions through federal payments of $150,000 per House seat, with appropriations of 'such sums as may be necessary' — roughly $65-80 million per decade nationally. The bigger cost falls on incumbent members of Congress and state legislative leaders of both parties, who lose the power to draw their own district lines and would see many safe seats become competitive.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and incumbent politicians of both parties

drawbacks.text: The bill is a federal mandate that overrides how states currently handle redistricting, and commission members would still be appointed by the majority and minority leaders of each state legislative chamber, so the 'independent' commission is partly built from partisan appointments [S3].

An evenly split commission appointed by both parties can deadlock, which is why the bill relies on court fallbacks — a state supreme court or federal district court picking the map — a slower and less democratic backstop [S3].
The federal payments are open-ended: each state gets $150,000 per House seat and the bill authorizes 'such sums as may be necessary' in appropriations [S3].
The rules would not apply until redistricting after the 2030 census, so nothing would change about the current congressional maps [S3].

Banning consideration of voting history and party affiliation except where needed for the Voting Rights Act can make it harder to draw districts that give minority communities real electoral power, a tension commissions would have to navigate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — politicians no longer choosing their own voters — is large for voters and directly aimed at a self-dealing practice that both major parties engage in where they control map-drawing. The costs are modest: tens of millions per decade in federal payments and a layer of new state machinery, plus the risk of partisan deadlocks resolved by courts rather than voters. The design has real weak points — commissioners appointed by legislative leaders, an open-ended appropriation, no effect until 2031 — but the substance goes at one of the clearer conflicts of interest in American elections.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, no one else signed on, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on April 17, 2023, naming it for John Tanner and Jim Cooper, two former Tennessee Democratic House members associated with redistricting reform [S1].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, which took no further action on it for the rest of the 118th Congress [S5].
No member of either party cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent members of Congress and the state legislators of both parties who currently control map-drawing keep that power, and the congressional maps in place for the rest of the decade stay as they are.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents who draw their own maps

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the only observable partisan fact is that a lone Democrat sponsored the bill and neither party produced a single cosponsor among the other 434 members.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislators (both parties)
industries.note: The bill removes map-drawing power from legislators and bars the commissions from protecting incumbent residences, converting many safe seats into competitive ones. Their interest in keeping that power runs directly against voters' interest in competitive elections.

industries.industry: Political redistricting consultants and map-drawing firms
industries.note: Legislative gerrymandering is a lucrative market for partisan map-drawing consultants and the data firms that serve them; commission-drawn maps under conflict-of-interest rules would shrink that business.
The agency would administer $150,000-per-seat payments to states and verify commission establishment before disbursing funds — a small administrative role, not a power grab.
